batch-A: OVERLAP WARNING (read first): batches B and D, written in parallel, already use several paintings and stories this brief suggested (bachiacca-manna, gozzoli-lazarus, blake-job-daughters, american-samaria, angeli-elijah-chariot, sustris-sea-galilee, tintoretto-paul), so batch A avoids all of them. One conflict remains: titian-patmos is used here for All Saints (1 Nov, Revelation 7) and by batch D on 12 Dec (Revelation 1 and 21). All Saints is the stronger claim; D should find another painting. B and D also clash with each other: bachiacca-manna, gozzoli-lazarus, angeli-elijah-chariot and domenichino-rebuke appear in both.

Stage ids 'learning-to-pray' and 'witnesses' are not yet in content/path.json. Suggested: learning-to-pray: title 'Learning to pray', line 'Daily bread, an honest cry, waiting, listening, letting go, a life turned, blessing.', why 'Having found your feet, you learn to talk to God, and to listen.' witnesses: title 'Witnesses', line 'People who saw something and said so.', why 'What you have received, you begin to pass on.'

Scripture: every verse and passage was checked against the WEB json in webrepo. As in the existing days, WEB's 'Yahweh' is kept verbatim (Exodus 17:4). The editorial guide says to write 'the Lord'; the reviewer should decide one rule for days.json. Small punctuation trims: Luke 2:29–30 ends at 'salvation' with the trailing comma dropped; Hebrews 11:38 begins mid-sentence ('of whom the world was not worthy…'), as WEB has it.

Passage lengths: several come to about 2 minutes by the helper's count (1 Kings 17:1-16, Exodus 17:1-16, Luke 2:22-40, Luke 22:31-46, Luke 7:36-50, Genesis 14:8-24, 2 Timothy 4:1-22, Esther 4:1-17, Mark 15:21-39, Matthew 10:16-33, Revelation 7:1-17, 1 Samuel 3:1-21). Hebrews 11:23-12:2 is a little longer. All are whole scenes; widen any of them if 3 minutes is a strict minimum.

19 Oct, Elijah: 1 Kings 17:1-6 (WEB). Savoldo, Elijah Fed by the Raven, c. 1510, NGA (already in art.json, not used by any day). The background chariot is in NGA's own description. Mendelssohn's Elijah, Part One: an Angel sends Elijah to the brook Cherith (recitative no. 6, then the double quartet 'For He shall give His angels'). Please check the numbering against a score. Horace, Odes 1.11 (Leuconoe; 'Babylonios numeros'; 'dum loquimur, fugerit invida aetas'; 'carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero'), Odes 1–3 published 23 BC.

20 Oct, Moses: Exodus 17:1-7, with 17:11-12 (Aaron and Hur) in read.why. Wtewael, Moses Striking the Rock, 1624, NGA (already in art.json; Wtewael worked in Utrecht). Family story water-from-the-rock (Exodus 17:1–7) is this very story. Psalm 13: four 'How long' questions in verses 1–2 (WEB); the attribution to David comes from the superscription. U2 '40' (War, 1983) sets Psalm 40 and closed their concerts for years; it ends with 'how long'. Only two words are quoted.

21 Oct, Simeon and Anna: Luke 2:22-38. 'About six weeks old': forty days after birth (Leviticus 12:2-4). The two birds are the poor family's offering (Leviticus 12:8; Luke 2:24). Anna's age: WEB says she had been a widow 'for about eighty-four years', which is why the text only says 'of great age'. Painting: Master of the Prado 'Adoration of the Magi', The Presentation in the Temple, c. 1470/1480, NGA. Anna is not named in NGA's description; the text describes the old woman behind the child without naming her. Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil, movement 5, is the Nunc dimittis ('Nyne otpushchayeshi'), which Rachmaninoff asked to have sung at his funeral. This is widely reported; please verify. Odyssey 17.290–327 (Argos).

22 Oct, Joan's vision: from the trial record, session of 22 February 1431. Joan said that at about thirteen she heard a voice from God at noon in summer in her father's garden, usually with a light, that she was very afraid, and that it told her to be good and go to church. She named Saints Michael, Catherine and Margaret in later sessions. Please check against a translation of the trial record, e.g. W. P. Barrett, The Trial of Jeanne d'Arc (1931), or the Quicherat edition. 'Could not read' is the usual view; she said so herself. Painting: Boutet de Monvel, The Vision and Inspiration (Joan of Arc series: I), c. 1907–early 1909, NGA (public domain; the painter died 1913). The sheep in the painting are the artist's; Joan testified that she did not usually tend the flocks. Plato, Apology 31c–d (the divine sign since childhood, which only holds him back and kept him out of politics) and 40a–c (it did not oppose his coming to court). 'Come Down, O Love Divine': Bianco da Siena (died 1434), translated by R. F. Littledale (1867).

23 Oct, Gethsemane: Luke 22:39-46 (WEB includes vv. 43–44, which some early manuscripts lack); read.why quotes Luke 22:32. Benvenuto di Giovanni, The Agony in the Garden, probably 1491, NGA. Its NGA series field is 'Passion of Our Lord' (a set of small panels). Seneca, Letter 107.10–11, quotes Cleanthes ('ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt'). Bach, St Matthew Passion: the tenor aria with chorus 'Ich will bei meinem Jesu wachen' follows the Gethsemane recitative.

24 Oct, Mary of Egypt: the Life attributed to Sophronius of Jerusalem (7th century). Details checked from memory and needing a check: Alexandria; about seventeen dissolute years; Jerusalem at the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross; held back at the church door; prayed before an icon of the Mother of God; crossed the Jordan; forty-seven years in the desert; Zosimas brought her communion on Holy Thursday at the Jordan; he found her dead a year later. The Orthodox commemorate her on the fifth Sunday of Great Lent. Ricci, The Last Communion of Saint Mary of Egypt, c. 1695, NGA. NOTE: she is shown naked from the waist up, holding a cloth to her chest. Please check it suits Pew; batch A has no other unused painting of a person at prayer if it is rejected. Verse: Luke 7:47, from a different woman's story, flagged as such. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.3. Allegri's Miserere sets Psalm 51.

25 Oct, Melchizedek: Genesis 14:17-20. Rubens, The Meeting of Abraham and Melchizedek, c. 1626, NGA. That it is a design (modello) for the Triumph of the Eucharist tapestries made for the Descalzas Reales convent in Madrid is from memory; please confirm on NGA's page. The painting does show the scene as a tapestry held up by putti. The link between Melchizedek and the Eucharist is ancient (e.g. Cyprian, Letter 63) and Hebrews 7 calls him a type of Christ. Virgil, Aeneid 8.102–369 (Evander's feast to Hercules; 'aude, hospes, contemnere opes', 8.364). Mozart, Ave verum corpus, 1791.

26 Oct, Peter: John 21:1-17 (six others named or counted in 21:2). Painting: Magnasco, Christ at the Sea of Galilee, c. 1740 (already in art.json, not used by any day). UNSURE: the subject could be John 21:7 (Peter wading to Jesus on the shore, with a boat at the mouth of the cove) or Matthew 14 (Peter sinking). Jesus stands on the shore, which fits John 21 better, but please check NGA's description. The charcoal fire: Greek 'anthrakia' appears only at John 18:18 and 21:9 in the New Testament. 'Morning Has Broken': Eleanor Farjeon, 1931.

27 Oct, Paul: 2 Timothy 4:6-18. Many scholars doubt that Paul wrote 2 Timothy, so the text says 'the last letter that bears his name'. 'Thirty years' runs roughly from conversion (c. AD 33–36) to death (c. 64–67). Rembrandt van Rijn (and Workshop?), The Apostle Paul, c. 1657, NGA, signed 'Rembrandt f.' The sword is his traditional emblem, after his beheading in Rome. Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy: imprisoned by Theodoric near Pavia, executed 524 or 525. Brahms, German Requiem, movement 6 sets 1 Corinthians 15:51–55.

28 Oct, Esther: Esther 4:10-16; 2:7 (cousin); 3:13 (the decree). In Esther 4 she and Mordecai speak only through the servant Hathach. Steenwijk shows them together in a church (an artistic licence), and NGA titles it simply 'Esther and Mordecai', so it may not be meant as chapter 4 exactly. Please check NGA's text. Signed 'H.V.S. 1616' (from NGA's description). Hebrew Esther never names God; the Greek additions do. Sophocles, Antigone, c. 441 BC (some date it 442). Salve Regina: 'exsules filii Hevae'.

29 Oct, Joan's trial: the trial opened in Rouen on 21 February 1431 (first public session), presided over by Bishop Pierre Cauchon. The grace answer is from the session of 24 February 1431. She was burned in Rouen on 30 May 1431, and the nullification verdict came on 7 July 1456. She was captured at Compiègne by Burgundian forces and handed to the English. 'Nineteen': born c. 1412. Boutet de Monvel, The Trial of Joan of Arc (series: VI), c. late 1909–early 1910, NGA. The man in the mitre is not named in the text. Acts 4:13, 19–20. Byrd, Mass for Four Voices, c. 1592–93, for recusant (secret Catholic) worship.

30 Oct, the centurion: Mark 15:33-39; Psalm 22:1. Cranach the Elder, The Crucifixion with the Converted Centurion, 1536, NGA. The inscriptions 'WARLICH DISER MENSCH IST GOTES SVN GEWEST' and 'VATER IN DEIN HET BEFIL ICH MEIN GAIST' are in NGA's description (Mark 15:39; Luke 23:46). Cranach was Luther's friend and godfather to his son. 'First human being in Mark to call Jesus Son of God': demons (3:11, 5:7) and the voice from heaven do so earlier, and the high priest asks it as a question (14:61). Plato, Republic 361e–362a (Glaucon; the verb is often translated 'impaled' or 'crucified').

31 Oct, Anthony and Paul: Jerome, Vita Pauli (c. 375–377). Anthony was about 90 and Paul 113; it was revealed to Anthony in the night; the centaur on the way; the raven bringing a whole loaf instead of half; Paul's death; Anthony buries him with the help of lions. Master of the Osservanza (Sano di Pietro?), The Meeting of Saint Anthony and Saint Paul, c. 1430/1435, NGA, one of a series on Anthony's life. NGA's description shows the centaur and the embrace. Hebrews 11:38. Herodotus 1.30 (Solon, Croesus, Tellus). Pärt, Spiegel im Spiegel, 1978.

1 Nov, All Saints: Revelation 7:9-17 and 1:9-10. That John of Patmos is John the apostle is traditional and debated, so the text says 'a follower of Jesus called John'; the eagle is the evangelist's emblem. The Orthodox keep All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost; the meaning says so, in line with the 'say which tradition keeps it' rule. Titian and Workshop, Saint John the Evangelist on Patmos, c. 1553/1555, NGA. That it was a ceiling painting for the Scuola Grande di San Giovanni Evangelista in Venice is from memory; please confirm. The painting shows John looking up at his vision, not the multitude itself. Cicero, De re publica 6 (Somnium Scipionis), c. 54–51 BC; Scipio Aemilianus meets Africanus and his father Paullus. 'For All the Saints': William Walsham How (1864), tune Sine Nomine by Vaughan Williams (1906).

Music: no piece is repeated within batch A. Several pieces are shared with other batches on different days (mendelssohn-elijah, u2-40, brahms-requiem, byrd-four-voices, spiegel, allegri-miserere, were-you-there, for-all-the-saints).
batch-B: Stage ids 'death-and-hope' and 'justice-and-mercy' are not yet in content/path.json; they need title, line and why added there.

Existing art.json works reused (not used by any day in days.json): angelico-entombment, poelenburch-elijah-widow, gozzoli-lazarus, perugino-crucifixion, benvenuto-resurrection, el-greco-martin, netherlandish-paralytic. Other batch writers may also reach for gozzoli-lazarus or benvenuto-resurrection; please check for clashes when merging.

All Souls' Day (2 Nov): kept by the Roman Catholic Church; in the Church of England's Common Worship calendar as 'Commemoration of the Faithful Departed (All Souls' Day)'; observed by many Lutherans. The Orthodox remember the dead on several 'Soul Saturdays' instead. Check wording 'Catholics, many Anglicans and Lutherans'.
John 19:38-42: Joseph of Arimathea a secret disciple; Nicodemus 'who at first came to Jesus by night' (John 3), about a hundred Roman pounds of myrrh and aloes. WEB text checked.
Antigone: Sophocles, first performed about 441 BC (date approximate, commonly given). Antigone buries Polynices against Creon's edict, appealing to the unwritten laws of the gods (lines c. 450-457).

Angelico entombment: NGA 'Attributed to Fra Angelico', c. 1450; artLink hedges ('perhaps Angelico himself'). The haloless man in red by the tomb is not identified in the NGA text; the 'see' does not name him. 'Two old men' carrying the body are not named by NGA; the 'see' avoids naming them as Joseph and Nicodemus.
Fauré Requiem: 'In Paradisum' is the antiphon traditionally sung as the body is taken from church to burial. Correct per the Latin funeral rite.
1 Kings 17:12 verse is the second half of the WEB verse (the first half contains the divine name). Text verbatim.

Luke 4:25-27: Jesus cites the widow of Zarephath in the Nazareth synagogue; the crowd drives him to the brow of the hill (Luke 4:28-30). Luke's Gospel dated 'about AD 80' (common scholarly estimate; some date it earlier).
Mendelssohn's Elijah (Birmingham, 1846): Part One includes the widow's plea ('What have I to do with thee, O man of God?') and the raising of her son. Please verify against a libretto.
Poelenburch: Dutch, worked in Rome in the 1610s-1620s (Utrecht Italianate). Date c. 1630 from NGA.
Gozzoli: NGA date 'mid 1490s'; Gozzoli died in 1497, so 'near the end of his long working life' is safe.
Plato, Phaedo 117c-e: Phaedo covers his face and weeps, Apollodorus cries aloud, Socrates says he sent the women away to avoid this and asks for quiet. Xanthippe is sent away at 60a.
Brahms, A German Requiem: first movement 'Selig sind, die da Leid tragen' (Matthew 5:4), as in music.json note.
Angeli: Giuseppe Angeli (1712-1798), Venetian; NGA date c. 1740/1755. 'Mounting corners' detail is from the NGA description.
Virgil, Aeneid 6.700-702: Aeneas tries three times to embrace Anchises' shade. Aeneid unfinished at Virgil's death, 19 BC; 'about 19 BC' refers to that.

Song for Athene: Tavener, 1993, in memory of Athene Hartley, a young family friend; text combines the Orthodox funeral service and Hamlet ('may flights of angels sing thee to thy rest', Hamlet 5.2, public domain).
Perugino: the Galitzin Triptych, c. 1482/1485, NGA. 'Disciple whom Jesus loved' kept as John's Gospel names him; the young man in the painting is identified by NGA title as Saint John.

Plutarch, Consolation to his Wife (Moralia 608A-612B): daughter Timoxena died aged about two while Plutarch was away; she asked the nurse to nurse other infants and even her toys; he praises his wife's restraint at the funeral. Date 'about AD 90' approximate.
Were You There: African American spiritual, first published in 1899 (Fisk/ William Barton collections are often cited); kept as 'the spiritual'.

Job: the friends sit seven days in silence (Job 2:13); God rebukes Eliphaz and the two friends (42:7); Job prays for them (42:10); daughters named and given inheritance (42:14-15). Job's ten children die in 1:18-19.

Blake, Job and His Daughters, 1799/1800, NGA (tempera, one of the biblical paintings Blake made for Thomas Butts; please check). Plate 20 of Blake's Illustrations of the Book of Job (1826) reworks this design: that is the last-but-one plate of 21 (incl. title page 22). Please verify the plate number. The reading that Job is telling his story (and that the wall panels show his trials) is the standard reading of the engraving; the 'see' only says 'as if telling a story' and that the panel figures are hard to make out.
Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison c. 523-524 before execution under Theodoric; Fortune's wheel is Book 2. Place: traditionally Pavia.
It Is Well: Spafford's four daughters drowned in the sinking of the Ville du Havre, 1873 (as in music.json).
Matthew 27:62-66 (guard posted, stone sealed) and 28:1-7. Remembrance Sunday 2026 is 8 November (second Sunday of November).

Benvenuto di Giovanni, The Resurrection, probably 1491, NGA; one of a series of Passion panels (NGA also holds his Agony in the Garden, Christ Carrying the Cross, Christ in Limbo). Please verify 'series'.
Thucydides 2.43: 'the whole earth is the tomb of famous men'; memory not only on inscriptions at home but unwritten in others' hearts. Funeral oration, winter 431/430 BC.
For All the Saints: words William Walsham How, 1864; tune Sine Nomine, Vaughan Williams, English Hymnal 1906.
Genesis 3:12 verse verbatim. Domenichino, The Rebuke of Adam and Eve, 1626, NGA.
Iliad 19.86-87: Agamemnon: 'I am not to blame, but Zeus and Fate and the Erinys who walks in darkness'. Homer dated 'about 750 BC' (conventional).

Allegri's Miserere sets Psalm 51; 'I know my transgressions; my sin is always before me' is the familiar wording of Psalm 51:3 (KJV-style). WEB has 'For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.' The music 'why' now uses the WEB wording.

Genesis 39 handled with discretion (no detail beyond the text). Rembrandt Workshop, Joseph Accused by Potiphar's Wife, 1655, NGA; Rembrandt's own 1655 version is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin. In the paintings Joseph is present at the accusation, which Genesis does not say: painter's licence. The red garment on the bedpost is not identified by NGA; 'see' does not call it Joseph's cloak.

Euripides, Hippolytus, 428 BC: Phaedra hangs herself and leaves a tablet accusing Hippolytus; Theseus curses him through Poseidon; Artemis reveals the truth. The echo says only that 'she dies' (in the play she hangs herself).
Messiaen, Quartet for the End of Time: composed in Stalag VIII-A, Görlitz; first performed there 15 January 1941.

St Martin: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin, ch. 3 (Amiens gate, winter, cloak cut with sword, bystanders laughed, dream of Christ in the half cloak saying 'Martin, still a catechumen, has clothed me with this robe', with reference to Matthew 25:40) and ch. 4 ('I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight', before Julian near Worms). Martin died 397; feast 11 November in the Western calendars (Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran). Armistice signed early on 11 November 1918, effective 11 am.

Matthew 25:40 verse: WEB text begins with an opening quotation mark (the verse opens a new paragraph of Jesus's speech); I dropped that leading mark only. The WEB json has a double space before 'you did it to me'; normalised to one space.
Using Matthew 25:40 as the verse only; the passage is Luke 6:27-49 to avoid clashing with Christ the King (22 Nov 2026, Year A gospel Matthew 25:31-46).
El Greco, Saint Martin and the Beggar, 1597/1599, NGA; painted for the Chapel of San José, Toledo. NGA also holds a workshop version (not used).
Cicero, De Officiis 1.51-52, quoting Ennius on lighting another's lamp; Cicero's rule of giving what can be given without loss. 44 BC.
Good King Wenceslas: J. M. Neale, 1853; last lines 'Ye who now will bless the poor / Shall yourselves find blessing' (public domain).
Mark 2:1-12: four carried him (2:3); 'seeing their faith' (2:5). Painting NGA 'Netherlandish 16th Century', c. 1560/1590; the NGA text describes the ropes and the people on the roof.
Seneca, De Clementia, addressed to Nero, AD 55-56; argues mercy most becomes a king/prince (1.3-1.5) and that a merciful ruler is guarded by his subjects' love (1.13, 1.19). Paraphrased.
Aretha Franklin, Amazing Grace: recorded January 1972 at New Temple Missionary Baptist Church, Los Angeles, with the Southern California Community Choir.

Garofalo, Christ Washing the Disciples' Feet, c. 1520/1525, NGA; Garofalo was from Ferrara. Identification of the haloless man with a pouch as Judas follows John 13:29 (Judas kept the money bag); NGA text describes the pouch and lack of halo but does not name him. Identification of the seated white-haired man as Peter follows John 13:6-9; NGA does not name him.
John 13:2 and 13:10-11: Jesus knew who would betray him; the text implies he washed all twelve including Judas (13:5, 13:12). Common reading; flag as interpretation.

Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.1. Book 1 ends with the note 'Among the Quadi, on the Granua' (some editions place it at the start of Book 2); 'on campaign on the Danube frontier, about AD 170s' hedges.
Ubi caritas: sung at the washing of feet on Maundy Thursday (as music.json). 'The priest' washing feet is the Catholic/Anglican practice; fine as general description.

Exodus 16:13-21; Paul quotes 16:18 in 2 Corinthians 8:15 when asking the Corinthians to give for the poor in Jerusalem. 'What is it?' is the WEB wording of 16:15 (the traditional explanation of the name manna, Exodus 16:31).

Bachiacca (Francesco d'Ubertino Verdi, 1494-1557), Florentine, known for animals and grotesques; NGA date 1540/1555. Animals listed are from the NGA description (it says 'cheetah-like animals'; I wrote 'spotted big cats', please check against the image).
Aristotle, Politics 2.5 (1263a): property private in ownership, common in use; proverb 'friends' things are common'; virtue/education rather than legislation makes it work. About 330 BC approximate.
Great Is Thy Faithfulness: Thomas Chisholm, 1923, based on Lamentations 3:22-23. Chisholm died 1960, so the words are in copyright: no lyrics quoted.

John 4: 'Jews have no dealings with Samaritans' (4:9); the disciples marvelled that he spoke with a woman (4:27); five husbands (4:18). I avoided the popular claim that she came at noon because she was shunned (debated).

Christ and the Woman of Samaria, American 18th Century, c. 1720/1740, NGA; likely one of the Hudson Valley biblical paintings based on Bible engravings (please check before saying so; artLink only says 'unknown American painter of the early 1700s').

Terence, Heauton Timorumenos (The Self-Tormentor), 163 BC, line 77, spoken by Chremes. Born in Carthage and brought to Rome as a slave, according to Suetonius's Life of Terence (hence 'said to have').
Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring: from Cantata BWV 147, Leipzig, 1723.
Family links: the-jar-that-never-ran-out (1 Kings 17:8-16), through-the-roof (Mark 2:1-12), the-last-supper (covers John 13:1-15 along with Luke 22; please confirm it is close enough).

Passages are 1-4 minutes by the helper's count; several (John 19:31-20:9, Matthew 27:62-28:10, Luke 6:27-49) cross chapters or run wider than the story to reach 3+ minutes. 'passage' is given as a ref string as the brief asks; build the paras with the web.py helper.
batch-C: STAGES: 'the-kingdom' and 'waiting' are not yet in content/path.json. Suggested entries: the-kingdom = title 'The kingdom', line 'Kingdoms refused, a peaceable kingdom, a king with a towel, a king on a cross.', why 'Jesus talked about the kingdom more than anything else. This part of the road asks what kind of king he is.' waiting = title 'Waiting', line 'Shut in the ark, bread for today, the long night, staying, watching, old eyes that see.', why 'Before Advent, the Bible's long waits, and what people found while nothing seemed to happen.'

PARABLES: the NGA open-access paintings (all 2,928 in the cache, checked by title and by assistivetext) contain no sower, mustard seed, pearl, treasure, wedding feast, talents, wise and foolish virgins, labourers in the vineyard, or Last Judgement / sheep and goats. The only parables are Lazarus and the rich man and the prodigal son, both already used. Tanner's 'The Good Shepherd' (tanner-shepherd) is too indistinct to show the lost sheep. Pilate: no painting shows Pilate; see the 20 Nov note. So the kingdom week is built on kingship stories with exact paintings. Also no NGA painting of Abraham and Sarah waiting, Zechariah, the rivers of Babylon or Habakkuk, so the waiting week uses Noah, the manna, Job, Elisha, Gethsemane, Simeon and Anna.

AVOIDED as likely overlaps: El Greco's Saint Martin and the Beggar (Matthew 25 lived out) was tempting for the sheep and goats, but St Martin's day (11 Nov) falls in another writer's week. The Expectant Madonna with Saint Joseph (French 15th C) and Domenico Veneziano's Saint John in the Desert were left for the Advent writers.

DIVINE NAME: the 23 Nov verse (Genesis 7:16) writes 'the Lord' for WEB's 'Yahweh', per EDITORIAL_GUIDE ('writing "the Lord" for the divine name'). All other verses are verbatim WEB and contain no divine name. Passages are given as refs only.

16 Nov, Temptation: Matthew 4:1-11. Painting: Juan de Flandes, The Temptation of Christ, c. 1500/1504, NGA. CHECK: that it is one of the small panels of the polyptych made for Queen Isabella of Castile (I believe NGA says so). The 'two tiny figures on the cliff' are described in the NGA alt text only as strokes that 'suggest two people'; the pair on the city tower is explicit. Echo: Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34, Prodicus' 'Choice of Heracles' (Vice says her friends call her Happiness, Eudaimonia). Written in the 370s BC ('about 370 BC'). Music: Be Thou My Vision, Eleanor Hull's versification (1912; Hull died 1935, public domain): 'Riches I heed not, nor man's empty praise' and 'High King of Heaven'.

17 Nov, Isaiah 11:1-9 (passage 11:1-10). Isaiah's ministry c. 740-700 BC ('about seven hundred years before Jesus'). Painting: Edward Hicks, Peaceable Kingdom, c. 1834. CHECK: Hicks a Quaker minister in Bucks County, Pennsylvania; painted the subject 60+ times (often given as about 62); the left background is Penn's Treaty with the Lenape (alt text describes the scene but does not name Penn); Hicks painted through the 1827 Hicksite separation among Quakers (his cousin Elias Hicks led one side). Echo: Virgil, Eclogue 4 (40 BC, Pollio's consulship), lines 21-25: goats bring home udders full of milk, herds will not fear great lions, the serpent will die. Constantine's Oration to the Assembly of the Saints, chs 19-21, read it as a prophecy of Christ. Music: O Come, O Come, Emmanuel, Neale's verse 'O come, Thou Rod of Jesse' (Isaiah 11:1, 10; the antiphon O Radix Jesse).

18 Nov, Genesis 14:17-24. Melchizedek = 'king of righteousness', Salem = 'peace' (Hebrews 7:2, WEB). Psalm 110:4 WEB: 'You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.' Painting: Rubens, The Meeting of Abraham and Melchizedek, c. 1626, NGA. CHECK: that it is the design (modello) for a tapestry in the Triumph of the Eucharist series commissioned by the Infanta Isabella for the Descalzas Reales convent, Madrid; the alt text confirms it is painted as a tapestry held up by putti. The alt text says 'oversized silver and gold urns'; I call them jars and do not say they hold wine. Echo: Plutarch, Life of Numa, esp. ch. 20 (temple of Janus shut for 43 years of Numa's reign); Numa chosen for wisdom and piety, founded Rome's priesthoods (Numa 3-9). Livy 1.19 gives a slightly different account of the Janus temple. Music: Mozart, Ave verum corpus, K. 618, June 1791, for Corpus Christi at Baden.

19 Nov, John 13:1-15 (passage 13:1-17). Painting: Garofalo, Christ Washing the Disciples' Feet, c. 1520/1525. The haloless man with a purse is identified as Judas by inference (alt text: no halo, pouch at belt, points at Jesus); John 12:6 and 13:29 say Judas kept the money box. Echo: Herodotus 2.172, Amasis and the golden footbath. Family: the-last-supper (stories.json, Luke 22:7-20; John 13:1-15) covers this story. Music: Ubi caritas, Duruflé 1960 (music.json); the antiphon is sung at the Maundy Thursday washing of feet.

20 Nov, John 18:33-19:3 (passage 18:28-19:5). PAINTING CAVEAT: there is no NGA open-access painting of Jesus before Pilate. Bachiacca, The Flagellation of Christ (c. 1512/1515), shows John 19:1, the flogging Pilate ordered straight after the dialogue; the retell ends on that moment and the artLink says so. Reviewer may prefer to swap the day. Echo: Epictetus, Discourses 1.1.22-24 (fetter my leg, not my will; prison for my body; did I say my neck alone could not be cut). Epictetus born a slave c. AD 50; Arrian's record usually dated c. AD 108, Nicopolis. Music: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (Salve caput cruentatum; Gerhardt 1656); the 'set it five times' claim repeats music.json's own note.

21 Nov, Clovis (non-biblical day, like the Francis and Jerome days). Source: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks 2.30-31: Clotilde's urging; the vow in battle against the Alamanni; baptism at Reims by Remigius; 'Bow your neck, Sicamber; adore what you have burned, burn what you have adored' (my wording keeps the sense). Date: traditionally Christmas 496, debated by historians (496-508), so 'around the year 500'. Painting: Master of Saint Giles, The Baptism of Clovis, c. 1500, NGA. CHECK the claim that he worked in Paris (generally described as a Netherlandish-trained painter active in Paris). The woman 'probably Clotilde' is my identification; alt text does not name her. The peacock as an early Christian sign of eternal life is standard iconography. Verse: Psalm 72:11. Echo: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.30 ('see that you are not made into a Caesar, not dyed with the purple... keep yourself simple, good, pure...'; 'life is short' from the same section). Music: Zadok the Priest, 1727, text from 1 Kings 1:38-40. The read.why says 'many scholars think' Philippians 2:6-11 is an early hymn.

22 Nov, CHRIST THE KING (Sunday next before Advent; Advent Sunday 2026 is 29 Nov). Instituted by Pius XI in 1925 (encyclical Quas primas), moved in 1969 to the last Sunday of the church year; kept by Catholics and by Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and other churches using the Revised Common Lectionary; not kept by the Orthodox. CHECK: Luke 23:33-43 is the feast's Gospel in Year C. 2026 is Year A (the Gospel is Matthew 25:31-46, the sheep and goats), so the retell avoids saying this passage is read today. I chose Luke because the NGA has no Last Judgement. Painting: Master of the Death of Saint Nicholas of Münster, Calvary, c. 1470/1480; the alt text confirms the angel taking the soul of the thief on our left, the demon on the right, and the entry into Jerusalem on a donkey in the distance. Echo: Seneca, De Clementia 1.3.3 (clemency suits no one more than a king or prince) and 1.5.4 (saving life is the mark of a great station). Written AD 55-56 for Nero. My sentence 'Anyone can take a life' paraphrases 1.5.4 loosely: please check. Music: Messiah, Hallelujah Chorus (Revelation 19:6, 11:15, 19:16).

23 Nov, Genesis 7:1-16 (passage 7:1-8:12). 'The rain would begin in seven days' (7:4, 7:10); 'God remembered Noah' (8:1 WEB). Painting: Turner, The Evening of the Deluge, c. 1843, NGA. The alt text calls the ark only an 'arched, copper-brown structure', with faint animal outlines that 'suggest a bear, crocodile, giraffe'; the title and the subject justify calling it the ark. CHECK: its relation to Tate's 'Shade and Darkness: The Evening of the Deluge' (exhibited 1843). Echo: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.313-415 (Deucalion and Pyrrha, small boat, Parnassus, Themis' oracle, stones become people); finished about AD 8. Family: noah-and-the-rainbow. Music: U2, '40' (War, 1983) sets Psalm 40:1-3.

24 Nov, Exodus 16:13-21 (passage 16:1-21). 'What is it?' is 16:15; white, 16:31; forty years, 16:35; 'Give us today our daily bread', Matthew 6:11 WEB. Painting: Bachiacca, The Gathering of Manna, 1540/1555; the animals are from the alt text, and 'a man with a stick points the way' is not named as Moses. Echo: Horace, Odes 1.11 (Leuconoe; Babylonian numbers; strain the wine; cut long hope short; carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero); Odes 1-3 published 23 BC. Music: Great Is Thy Faithfulness (Lamentations 3:22-23); lyrics (Chisholm, 1923) still in copyright, so none are quoted.

25 Nov, Job 42 (verse 42:5; daughters 42:13-15; prays for friends 42:10). Painting: William Blake, Job and His Daughters, 1799/1800, NGA (tempera, I believe one of the biblical temperas made for Thomas Butts). 'He came back to Job's story again and again' refers to the Butts watercolours (c. 1805-10) and the engraved Illustrations of the Book of Job (1826). 'Blake shows him telling them his story' follows Job 42 and Blake's design; the alt text says only that the wall pictures show indistinct figures. Echo: Aeschylus, Agamemnon 176-183 ('learning through suffering', pathei mathos; pain dripping before the heart in sleep; wisdom comes to the unwilling), produced 458 BC. Music: Brahms, A German Requiem, movement 2 sets James 5:7 ('So seid nun geduldig'); James 5:11 WEB has 'the perseverance of Job'.

26 Nov, 2 Kings 2:1-12 (passage 2:1-14). Verse is the first sentence of 2:12, verbatim WEB. 'Yes, I know it. Hold your peace.' is 2:3/2:5 WEB. Painting: Giuseppe Angeli, Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire, c. 1740/1755. CHECK: Angeli Venetian (pupil of Piazzetta). Echo: Ruth 1:8-17 (Naomi urges her to turn back in 1:8, 11, 12, 15; Ruth 1:16); set 'in the days when the judges judged' (Ruth 1:1). Pastoral note: the day touches on keeping watch at a deathbed; no specific crisis content. Music: Mendelssohn, Elijah, Part 2 chorus 'Then did Elijah the prophet break forth like a fire' ('...a fiery chariot, with fiery horses; and he went by a whirlwind to heaven').

27 Nov, Matthew 26:36-46 (passage 26:30-56). 26:33-35 Peter's promise, 26:56 'all the disciples left him, and fled'. Painting: Benvenuto di Giovanni, The Agony in the Garden, probably 1491, NGA, one of a series of Passion panels (NGA also holds his Crucifixion, Christ in Limbo, Resurrection and Christ Carrying the Cross). The angel with the cup comes from Luke 22:43 and the tradition, not from Matthew. Echo: Plato, Crito 43a-b (Crito arrives before dawn, watches Socrates sleep and marvels at how peacefully he sleeps). Music: St Matthew Passion, tenor aria with chorus 'Ich will bei meinem Jesu wachen' / 'So schlafen unsre Sünden ein' (no. 20 in the NBA numbering), in the Gethsemane scene.

28 Nov, Luke 2:22-38 (passage 2:22-40). 'About six weeks': the purification of Leviticus 12:2-4, 40 days after a boy's birth. 'Offering of the poor': Luke 2:24 with Leviticus 12:8. Anna 'of great age' (2:36-37). Painting: Master of the Prado 'Adoration of the Magi', The Presentation in the Temple, c. 1470/1480, NGA. The figures are identified from the alt text (man in purple holding the baby, old woman behind the baby, old man with a cane and birdcage) and named by me as Simeon, Anna and probably Joseph. Echo: Cicero, Cato Maior de Senectute 7.24-25 (the farmer planting for the immortal gods, who wished him to receive from his ancestors and hand on to posterity), 44 BC. Music: Rachmaninoff, All-Night Vigil, no. 5, 'Nyne otpushchayeshi' (Nunc dimittis), whose basses descend to a low B flat. CHECK: Rachmaninoff asked for it at his funeral (widely reported). The English 'Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace' is the Book of Common Prayer (public domain). 'Sung at evening prayer for centuries' refers to Compline and Anglican Evensong.
FOCUS values for the 13 new paintings are my estimates from the alt-text layout. Please check the crops.
batch-D: Scripture: every story.verse was copied programmatically from the WEB JSON (whitespace normalised). Genesis 3:9 renders WEB 'Yahweh God' as 'The Lord God', per EDITORIAL_GUIDE rule 2; all passages are given as ranges only and keep the WEB text when expanded.

Dates: 29 Nov 2026 is Advent Sunday (Christmas Day 2026 is a Friday, so the four Sundays before are 29 Nov, 6, 13, 20 Dec); 6 Dec is the Second Sunday of Advent and St Nicholas's Day; 30 Nov is St Andrew's Day. 8 Dec (Catholic feast of the Immaculate Conception) is deliberately not named.

Paintings: all eleven newArt works are open-access NGA paintings not in art.json; tintoretto-paul, gozzoli-lazarus and titian-patmos are existing art.json works not used by any day in days.json (titian-patmos and gozzoli-lazarus appear in journeys.json; please check no other batch has taken them). 'see' texts are drawn only from the NGA assistivetext.

11-29 Veneziano, Saint John in the Desert: artLink says it was a small panel beneath an altarpiece; it is a predella panel from the St Lucy Altarpiece (Santa Lucia de' Magnoli, Florence). Please confirm on the NGA object page. The scene (John leaving his clothes for the desert) is traditional, based on Luke 1:80, not a Gospel narrative.

11-30 St Andrew: NGA has no open-access painting of John 1:35-42, so the day follows the pattern of 4 Oct (St Francis): the saint's life, with a painting of the saint (Agnolo Gaddi, left wing of a triptych, shortly before 1387; the inscription reads S. ANDREAS). The image is small (2152 px wide). Flag: the painting is a standing saint with his cross and a rope, not a narrative moment; the reviewer may prefer to drop it. 'Tradition says he died on a cross at Patras' (Acts of Andrew; Golden Legend). The rope is usually read as his being tied, not nailed, to the cross: I kept this out of 'see' and only describe the rope. Andrew bringing the boy with loaves (John 6:8-9) and the Greeks (John 12:20-22) checked in WEB. Crimond is a village in Aberdeenshire; Andrew is patron saint of Scotland.

11-30 echo: Plutarch, De fraterno amore (Moralia), ch. 2 on paired parts of the body (hands, feet, eyes) as a model for brothers; later chapters advise against envy between brothers when one is more honoured. Date about AD 100 is approximate.

12-01 Willem Reuter (c. 1642-1681), Flemish, born Brussels, worked in Rome: check. Luke 3:7-14 content checked in WEB. Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 5.6 (the vine that bears grapes and seeks nothing more). Book 5 has no place heading, so 'when' is kept general (AD 170-180). Wachet auf BWV 140: the opening chorus is the watchmen's call from the tower.

12-02 Giuseppe Angeli (1712-1798), Venetian, pupil of Piazzetta. Elisha's threefold 'I will not leave you' (2 Kings 2:2,4,6); Malachi 4:5 (last words of the Christian Old Testament order); Matthew 11:14 (John is Elijah). Aeneid 2: Aeneas carries Anchises, who holds the sacra/household gods (Penates), leading Iulus by the hand. Mendelssohn's Elijah, Part 2, chorus 'Then did Elijah the prophet break forth like a fire' sings of the fiery chariot and whirlwind: please check the number.

12-03 Juan de Flandes, The Temptation of Christ, c. 1500/1504: one of the small panels of the polyptych painted for Isabella of Castile. Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34, the Choice of Heracles after Prodicus; Virtue's words that the gods grant nothing good without toil and care are in 2.1.28. Matthew 4:16 quotes Isaiah 9 ('the people who sat in darkness saw a great light'). 'Be Thou My Vision' (Hull's versification) has the line 'Riches I heed not, nor man's empty praise': referred to, not quoted.

12-04 Gozzoli, The Feast of Herod and the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, 1461-1462: a predella panel; artLink says 'in Florence': Gozzoli was Florentine but please confirm where it was painted (I am not sure of the altarpiece's original location). Antigone c. 441 BC (traditional date); she is shut alive in a rocky tomb/cave; Creon relents too late. Byrd's Mass for Four Voices c. 1592-3 for recusant worship; Byrd was repeatedly fined as a recusant.

12-05 Domenichino (Domenico Zampieri, 1581-1641), born Bologna, worked mainly in Rome; NGA date 1626. Genesis 3:15 as the 'protoevangelium' (first gospel) is a long Christian reading (Irenaeus onwards); stated as 'Christians have long called it'. Hesiod, Works and Days 42-105: Pandora's jar, Hope (Elpis) stays under the rim. Haydn's Creation Part III is Adam and Eve in Eden.

12-06 Painting: NGA 'Circle of Jacopo Tintoretto (Probably Lambert Sustris)', c. 1570s; Venice is assumed from the attribution. magnasco-sea-galilee (art.json) is a different painting of a similar subject: avoid giving both to days. Matthew 14:25 'fourth watch of the night' (about 3-6 am). St Nicholas is patron saint of sailors. Odyssey 5: Poseidon wrecks the raft; Ino/Leucothea gives the veil (kredemnon); two nights and days in the sea. U2 '40' (War, 1983) sets Psalm 40.

12-07 Veronese, The Finding of Moses, c. 1581/1582 (NGA). Exodus 1:15-21 midwives; 1:22 order; 2:1-10. Livy 1.4: Amulius orders the twins thrown into the Tiber, flood leaves them in the shallows, she-wolf, shepherd Faustulus and wife Larentia. Vivaldi's Gloria RV 589 is generally thought to have been written for the Ospedale della Pietà, a foundling home: 'generally thought' may be the safer wording. Family story: the-baby-in-the-basket.

12-08 Bachiacca (Francesco d'Ubertino Verdi, 1494-1557), Florentine. 'Manna' as 'What is it?' (Exodus 16:15, 31). Horace, Odes 1.11 (to Leuconoe), 'carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero'; about 23 BC (Odes 1-3 published). Matthew 6:11 WEB 'Give us today our daily bread.' Great Is Thy Faithfulness: Lamentations 3:22-23.

12-09 Tintoretto, The Conversion of Saint Paul, c. 1544 (art.json). The figure in the clouds is identified only as 'a bearded figure', since the NGA text does not name him. Plato, Republic 7, 515c-516b, the freed prisoner dazzled. John Newton was master of slave ships before his ordination.

12-10 Gozzoli, The Raising of Lazarus, mid 1490s (art.json); Gozzoli c. 1421-1497. John 11:9-10, 11:44 'Free him, and let him go.' Euripides, Alcestis, produced 438 BC; Heracles wrestles Thanatos. O Come, O Come, Emmanuel (Neale): verse 'O come, thou Dayspring... and death's dark shadows put to flight'.

12-11 Benvenuto di Giovanni, Christ in Limbo, probably 1491: one of a set of predella-like panels at the NGA with Christ Carrying the Cross and The Resurrection (both in art.json). The story is not a single Bible narrative: it rests on Isaiah 9:2, 1 Peter 3:18-19 and 4:6, the creeds ('he descended to the dead / into hell'), and the Gospel of Nicodemus (Descent into Hell), which itself quotes Isaiah 9. In 'meaning' I say the old man with the hoe 'seems to be' Adam: an interpretation (Adam is traditionally first to be raised; the hoe recalls Genesis 3:23), please check. Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.1-77 (Orpheus and Eurydice). MacMillan's 'O Radiant Dawn' (2007) sets the O Oriens antiphon, 'shine on those who dwell in darkness and the shadow of death'.

12-12 Titian and Workshop, Saint John the Evangelist on Patmos, c. 1553/1555: painted for the ceiling of the Scuola Grande di San Giovanni Evangelista, Venice (artLink says only 'a ceiling in Venice'). Revelation 1:9-10 (Patmos, 'the Lord's day'); 21:22-25; 22:5. Cicero, De re publica 6.9-29 (Somnium Scipionis): Africanus appears; the earth seen as tiny; a place in heaven for those who preserve their country; fame is fleeting. Holy, Holy, Holy draws on Revelation 4.

Passages: all WEB ranges; reading times from the helper are 2-4 minutes. Some are at the short end (Luke 3:1-22, Mark 6:14-29, Matthew 14:13-33, Acts 9:1-22, Isaiah 8:19-9:7), in line with existing 2-minute days.
Stages 'prepare-the-way' and 'light-in-darkness' are not yet in content/path.json: they need adding (title, line, why).
batch-E: Calendar: 13 Dec 2026 = Third Sunday of Advent (Gaudete); 20 Dec = Fourth Sunday; Christmas Day is a Friday. O Antiphons: 18 Dec O Adonai (God who appeared to Moses in the burning bush), 19 Dec O Radix Jesse (Isaiah 11), 21 Dec O Oriens (Morning Star / Dawn). Rose-pink candle on Gaudete is a custom of many, not all, churches.

St Lucy (13 Dec): martyr of Syracuse, died about 304. Claim that in the old (Julian) calendar her feast fell on what was reckoned the shortest day: cf. John Donne, 'A Nocturnal upon St Lucy's Day, Being the Shortest Day'. Kept light as asked.
21 Dec 2026 is the December solstice (about 20:50 UTC), so 'shortest day / longest night' holds for the northern hemisphere. Check if the app serves the southern hemisphere.

duccio-nativity (existing art id): NGA inscription data: Isaiah's scroll = Isaiah 7:14 (Ecce virgo concipiet... Emanuel); the angel's scroll to the shepherds = 'Annuntio vobis gaudium magnum' (variant of Luke 2:10). Front predella of the Maestà, Siena Cathedral, begun by Oct 1308, installed 1311.

expectant-madonna-joseph (new): NGA 'The Expectant Madonna with Saint Joseph', French 15th century, c. 1425/1450. It shows Mary pregnant with Joseph behind a curtain, which fits Matthew 1:18–19; the painting is not explicitly titled 'Joseph's doubt'. Reviewer may judge whether it counts as 'that exact moment'.

signorelli-marriage (new): Signorelli, The Marriage of the Virgin, c. 1490/91. Used for Matthew 1:24 ('took his wife to himself'). Matthew does not describe a wedding; the priest, broken rods and suitors come from later legend (Protevangelium / Golden Legend), which the artLink and 'see' say plainly. Flag: weakest painting-to-moment match in the batch.

baronzio-naming-john (new): NGA inscription on Zechariah's sheet 'NOMEN EST IOHANNES'. Shows birth, naming and circumcision of John (Luke 1:57–64), not the adult Baptist. Baronzio was a Rimini painter.

lippi-nativity (new): Fra Filippo Lippi and Workshop, The Nativity, probably c. 1445. Used for the arrival at Bethlehem (Luke 2:1–6): Joseph asleep with a staff and tied sack on his shoulder. The baby is already born in the painting, so it shows the journey's end, which the artLink says.
veronese-finding-moses (new): Veronese c. 1581/82. 'Dressing Pharaoh's daughter as a Venetian lady' is my description of the brocade, pearls and tiara in the alt text.

hicks-peaceable-kingdom (new): Edward Hicks (1780–1849), Quaker preacher of Bucks County, Pennsylvania, painted about 60 versions of Peaceable Kingdom. The background group is Penn's treaty with the Lenape (NGA description; alt text says only indigenous people and men in tricorn hats, so 'see' describes it neutrally). Claim that he kept painting it through the quarrels that split the Quakers (the 1827 Hicksite separation, led by his cousin Elias Hicks): please check wording.

botticelli-adoring, bassano-shepherds, juan-flandes-nativity (existing ids, not used by any day). Juan de Flandes: altarpiece of San Lázaro, Palencia, commissioned c. 1508 (NGA provenance); the angel's banner reads GLOR... IN EXCELSIS DEO.

isenbrant-shepherds (new): Adriaen Isenbrant, probably 1520/1540; he worked in Bruges. mengs-shepherds (new): c. 1764/65, commissioned as altarpiece for the private chapel of Charles III of Spain (NGA provenance). The alt text notes tears in Mary's eyes. christus-nativity (new): Petrus Christus c. 1450 (Bruges). The alt text describes 'a nude man atop a column' and 'a similar woman'; NGA's catalogue identifies them as Adam and Eve and the two pairs of men as shepherds. Please check.
Seneca, Letter 41.1: 'God is near you, he is with you, he is within you' (Gummere, 1917): no need to lift hands to heaven or ask a temple keeper to reach the idol's ear.
Cicero, De Officiis 1.33 (1.10.33): 'summum ius summa iniuria', which he calls an already well-worn proverb. My rendering is 'the more law, the more injustice'.
Genesis 37–50 (Joseph the dreamer, Egypt, famine); Matthew 1:16 (Jacob the father of Joseph); Matthew 2:13–14 (flight to Egypt).

Plutarch, De garrulitate (On Talkativeness), Moralia: the saying that we learn speech from men but silence from the gods. I'm confident the idea is in this essay but have not checked the exact section. Please verify.

Augustus, Res Gestae 8: three censuses (28 BC, 8 BC, AD 14) with totals of 4,063,000, 4,233,000 and 4,937,000 citizens. The text was set up on bronze pillars outside his Mausoleum. The text does NOT claim Luke's census was one of these; the historicity and date of Luke's census (Quirinius, AD 6) are debated.
Nazareth to Bethlehem: roughly 80–90 miles (about 130–145 km) depending on route.

Livy 1.4: Amulius orders the twins drowned; servants leave them in a trough or basket at the edge of the flooded Tiber; a thirsty she-wolf hears the crying and suckles them; the shepherd Faustulus takes them home.

Virgil, Eclogue 4 (about 40 BC): a child, the return of the golden age, goats coming home with full udders, herds not fearing great lions, the serpent dying. The Christian messianic reading: Constantine's Oration to the Saints; Dante, Purgatorio 22 (Statius).
Handel's Messiah: first performed in Dublin, 1742, for charity; Part 1 opens with Isaiah 40 ('Comfort ye') and includes Isaiah 9:6.
Homer, Odyssey 14: Eumaeus welcomes the disguised Odysseus, makes a bed of brushwood and goatskin, roasts two piglets, and says strangers and beggars are from Zeus (about lines 49–58, 72–80).
Homer, Iliad 8.555–559: the simile of the stars round the bright moon on a windless night, with the shepherd glad at heart.
Plato, Republic 10.617b (the Myth of Er): a Siren on each of the eight circles, each singing one note, together making one harmony.
1 Samuel 16:1–13: Samuel in Bethlehem; seven sons of Jesse passed over; David the youngest, keeping the sheep.
Augustine, Confessions 10.8 ('fields and spacious palaces of memory', Pusey) and 10.24–27 (finding God in memory).
Heraclitus, fragment DK B1 (the Logos that people fail to understand, as if asleep). John's link to Ephesus: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1.

Music: o-come-emmanuel (the Immanuel name); wachet-auf (link is the theme of waking, not this text); spiegel (Pärt's years of silence, per music.json); christmas-oratorio (Part I sets Luke 2:1, 3–6); u2-40 (Psalm 40:1–2, paraphrased, no lyrics); o-magnum-mysterium (the text speaks of animals seeing the newborn Lord in a manger); o-radiant-dawn (O Oriens, sung on 21 Dec); vivaldi-gloria (Gloria in excelsis = Luke 2:14; written for the Ospedale della Pietà); in-the-bleak-midwinter (Rossetti's last verse, paraphrased); silent-night (Oberndorf, Christmas Eve 1818); o-come-all-ye-faithful (Christmas Day verse 'Word of the Father, now in flesh appearing', traditionally sung only on Christmas Day; Oakeley/public domain).

The 15 Dec verse (Matthew 1:24) ends with a semicolon in the WEB because the sentence continues into v.25; I replaced it with a full stop. All other verses are taken verbatim from the WEB json by script.

Family: 18 Dec uses the-baby-in-the-basket (Exodus 2:1–10) and 24 Dec uses the-shepherds (Luke 2:1–20). The 24 Dec passage is Luke 2:1–20, which is also a journey reading; the day's emphasis is Mary pondering (2:19). The 20 Dec passage (Luke 2:1–7) overlaps the 17 Dec story (Luke 2:1–6) on purpose: the 17th's long read is Micah 5, and the emphases differ (the census and road, then 'no room').
Stage ids 'god-comes-close' and 'christmas' are not yet in content/path.json (it has five stages so far).
batch-R: SKIPPED 2026-12-05 (prepare-the-way) and 2026-12-18 (god-comes-close): no open-access NGA painting with usable alt text shows a fitting, unused story. Civerchio's 'Christ Instructing Peter and John to Prepare for the Passover' (Luke 22:7-13, ideal for prepare-the-way) has no assistivetext and the image could not be viewed (api.nga.gov blocked), so it was not used. The Annunciation, Visitation, Joseph's dreams, Zechariah and the road to Bethlehem are already used in bank.json.

Paintings reused from art.json (not used by any day in bank.json, but used by a theme/library/playlist entry): veronese-rebecca, catholic-kings-cana, bassano-draught-fishes, carpaccio-flight, koerbecke-ascension, osservanza-anthony-alms, blake-supper. New: heiligenkreuz-clare, angelico-palladia, castagno-david, tintoretto-golden-calf, bartolo-joachim-anna, veronese-lucy. All 'see' text is drawn from the NGA assistivetext; interpretive touches are hedged ('probably her soul', 'most likely Moses').

Scripture: every 'verse' is verbatim WEB from the local json, so 'Yahweh'/'Yah' is kept (Genesis 24:15 has none; 1 Samuel 17:47 has Yahweh; Psalm 113:9 ends 'Praise Yah!'). Retellings paraphrase and use no quotation marks except Mary's 'They have no wine' in the midday line (John 2:3 WEB).

Oct 21 Rebecca: Genesis 24:10-27 (ten camels v10; evening, women drawing water v11; prayer vv12-14; 'before he had finished' v15; gold ring and two bracelets v22; bowed and worshipped vv26-27). 'One of the first prayers for guidance in the Bible' is a soft claim; check. Echo: Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.3.2 (Socrates prayed simply for 'good things'; praying for gold, silver or power was like praying for a throw of dice). Date 'about 370 BC' is approximate for composition. Veronese died 1588; NGA dates the painting c. 1582/1588 'Veronese and Workshop'.

Oct 25 Cana: John 2:1-11 ('the third day' 2:1; six stone jars 2:6; filled to the brim 2:7; 'kept the good wine until now' 2:10). Echo: Augustine, Letter 130 to Proba (c. AD 411/412), 8.17: God knows our will; we pray so our desire is exercised to receive what he prepares. Music: BWV 147 chorale 'Jesus bleibet meine Freude'. Master of the Catholic Kings: named after Ferdinand and Isabella; the NGA panels are dated c. 1495/1497; please check my artLink against NGA's object page. Tablecloth inscription per NGA alt text (AVE GRACIA PLENA...). It is a Sunday; no calendar named.

Nov 5 Clare: Clare left home in 1212 (Palm Sunday night), lived at San Damiano until her death on 11 August 1253; long illness (about 28 years). Last words per the Legend of St Clare (attributed to Thomas of Celano, c. 1255), ch. 46, and the Acts of the Process of Canonisation: 'Go calmly in peace... He who created you... has always guarded you as a mother who loves her child... Blessed be You, O Lord, who created me.' Vision of virgins in white with gold crowns, the most beautiful embracing/covering her, from the same Legend (Sister Benvenuta). Painting: Master of Heiligenkreuz, c. 1400/1410; 'Austrian' should be checked against NGA. Echo: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.48 (ripe olive falling, blessing nature and thanking the tree), checked against the Casaubon text in scratchpad. Music quote 'Come, enjoy rewards and crowns I have prepared for you' is the last line of Tavener's text (from the Orthodox funeral service); under 25 words.

Nov 13 Cosmas and Damian: Golden Legend, ch. on Saints Cosmas and Damian (feast 27 Sept): twin physicians of Aegea in Cilicia who took no fees; Palladia, who had spent all she had on doctors, offered Damian a small gift; he took it when she adjured him by God; Cosmas ordered he not be buried with him; that night the Lord appeared to Cosmas and excused Damian; after their martyrdom (under Diocletian) they were buried together (the Legend adds a camel that spoke to say so; omitted). Fra Angelico panel: predella of the San Marco altarpiece, Florence, c. 1438/1440; Cosmas and Damian were the Medici patron saints; check the 'Medici paid for it' phrasing. Echo: Plutarch, De fraterno amore 17 (488B-C): Pythagoreans reconciled before sunset; Plutarch mentions his brother Timon in the same essay. Music: 'Cessent iurgia maligna, cessent lites' is in the full Ubi caritas hymn, not in Duruflé's motet text, hence 'its fuller verses'.

Nov 17 David: 1 Samuel 17 (forty days v16; youngest v14; food for brothers vv17-18; Saul's clothing, bronze helmet, coat of mail v38; five smooth stones v40; stone sank into forehead v49). Castagno: NGA dates c. 1450/1455; it is painted on a leather ceremonial/parade shield (check NGA wording). Echo: Livy 7.9-10, Titus Manlius Torquatus and the Gaul at the Anio bridge, 361 BC; foot soldier's shield and Spanish sword; took the torque. 'A king born among animals in Bethlehem' refers to Luke 2:7 manger.

Nov 24 Draught of fishes: Luke 5:1-11. Family story the-net-full-of-fish is also attached to matthew-4-leaving-the-nets (Oct 6), a different call story; drop it here if each family story should appear once. Echo: Virgil, Aeneid 1.198-209 ('O socii...', forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit; durate et vosmet rebus servate secundis; spem vultu simulat), checked against Dryden in scratchpad. Bassano 1545 per NGA.

Nov 25 Flight: Matthew 2:13-15, 19-21. An infancy story before Advent, like Simeon on 28 Nov. Echo: Cicero exiled March 58 BC, mostly at Thessalonica (also Dyrrachium); recalled by law of 4 August 57 BC; returned to Rome 4 September 57 to welcoming crowds (Ad Atticum 4.1); despairing letters in Ad Atticum Book 3 (e.g. 3.7, 3.9, wishing he had died). Family: the-journey-by-night (Matthew 2:13-23).

Nov 26 Golden calf: Exodus 24:17-18 (fire on the mountain; forty days), 32:1-8 (calf; feast next day; God tells Moses), 32:11-14 (Moses pleads). The kneeling figure in flames at top right is described in NGA alt only as 'a person... flames'; identified here as 'most likely Moses'. The man in the crescent headdress may be Aaron; not named. Tintoretto died 31 May 1594; painting is 'Workshop of Jacopo Tintoretto', c. 1594. Echo: Odyssey 10 (bag of winds; nine days, tenth day home in sight; Odysseus asleep; crew open it), checked against Pope's translation in scratchpad. Music: Heber verse 3 'Though the darkness hide thee, though the eye of sinful man thy glory may not see' (public domain).

Nov 27 Ascension: Acts 1:3-14. 'About ten days' from Ascension (40th day) to Pentecost (50th day) is inference from Acts 1:3 and 2:1. Koerbecke: Marienfeld altarpiece (Westphalia), 1456/1457; check 'high altar of the monastery church'. Bearded figures on the clouds (tablets, harp) are probably Old Testament figures; only the objects are named. Echo: Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.805-828 (Mars carries off Romulus while he gives judgements; body dissolves like a lead sling-bullet; becomes Quirinus). Mentions that Advent begins on Sunday 29 November 2026.

Dec 3 Anthony: Athanasius, Life of Antony 2-3 (about 18-20 when parents died; within six months; heard Matthew 19:21 read on entering church; gave 300 arourae of land to villagers; sold the rest for the poor, keeping a little for his sister; later gave the rest after hearing Matthew 6:34). Athanasius wrote c. AD 360. Same Osservanza series as 'anthony-finds-paul' (Oct 31); different episode and panel. Echo: Diogenes Laertius 6.87 (Crates turned his property into money and distributed it to his fellow citizens); DL dated 3rd century AD (approximate). Music: Eleanor Hull's 1912 versification, 'Riches I heed not, nor man's empty praise'.

Dec 8 Joachim and Anna: names from the Protevangelium of James (2nd century); the threefold division of goods and the twenty childless years are from the Golden Legend's chapter on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary (Joachim's offering refused at the Feast of Dedication; he went to his shepherds; an angel to each; meeting at the Golden Gate). Catholic Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception, 8 December; Orthodox 'Conception by St Anna of the Most Holy Theotokos', 9 December. Andrea di Bartolo, c. 1400/1405; NGA also holds his Presentation of the Virgin and Nativity of the Virgin of the same date, so 'one of a series on the life of Mary' seems safe but check. Echo: Seneca, De beneficiis 4.26.1 ('if you imitate the gods... give even to the ungrateful; the sun rises on the wicked, the seas are open to pirates'). Music: Bogoroditse Devo is movement 6 of the Vigil. The verse (Psalm 113:9) ends 'Praise Yah!', verbatim WEB.

Dec 10 Last Supper: Matthew 26:14-30 (thirty pieces of silver v15; 'one of you will betray me' v21; bread v26; cup for remission of sins v28). Blake, 1799, tempera; one of the c. 50 biblical temperas for Thomas Butts (1799-1800); check against NGA. The man counting coins is in the NGA alt. Family the-last-supper is also attached to the-king-with-a-towel (Nov 19); drop here if each should appear once. Echo: Tacitus, Annals 15.62 ('imaginem vitae suae'; tablets for his will refused), written c. AD 116; Seneca died AD 65. Music: Ave verum corpus, June 1791; Mozart died 5 December 1791.

Dec 12 Lucy: Golden Legend, St Lucy (13 Dec): Syracuse; mother healed at St Agatha's tomb in Catania; patrimony given to the poor; betrothed denounced her to Paschasius; immovable by men and oxen; stabbed with a sword (the Legend says the throat; Veronese paints the chest); did not die until priests brought the Body of the Lord. Martyred c. 304 under Diocletian. Name from lux (traditional, and given by the Golden Legend). Julian-calendar drift put 13 Dec near the solstice in the late Middle Ages (cf. Donne's 'Nocturnal upon St Lucy's Day, being the shortest day'). Candle processions: Sweden, Norway, Finland. Note that E's 13 Dec day (immanuel-god-with-us) also mentions St Lucy; the two fit together but a reviewer may want to trim one mention. Veronese c. 1585/1586 (died 1588). Echo: Epictetus, Discourses 1.1.23-24 (checked against the scratchpad translation); Arrian recorded the Discourses at Nicopolis c. AD 108.

Calendar named only on real feasts: Immaculate Conception / Conception by St Anna (Dec 8, traditions named) and the eve of St Lucy (Dec 12); Advent mentioned on Nov 27 and Dec 3. Oct 25 is a Sunday; no feast named.

Echo authors across the batch: Xenophon, Augustine, Marcus Aurelius, Plutarch, Livy, Virgil, Cicero, Homer, Ovid, Diogenes Laertius, Seneca, Tacitus, Epictetus (each once). Music ids all exist in music.json; first uses for every-grain-of-sand, song-for-athene, hallelujah, holy-holy-holy, haydn-creation.
